utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is being resumed. Let me ask Mr. Registrar to call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, indictment IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Can we have the appearances for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours, Counsel, and everyone in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution, Ms. Tecla Henry-Benjamin, Mr. Kyle Wood, Ms. Ruth Karper, our case manager, and Daryl Mundis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of General Enver Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, counsel; Stephane Bourgon, co-counsel; and Muriel Cauvin, legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And for Mr. Kubura.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Kubura, Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and Nermin Mulalic, legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The Chamber wishes to greet all those present, the representatives of the Prosecution, and especially Madam Benjamin, who is present today, Mr. Mundis, and the counsel for the Defence, the accused. I also wish to greet our new registrar, who has just taken over his position and who will be assisting us during future hearings. I also wish to greet the usher, who has a very important role, as we all know, as well as all the staff of this courtroom, the interpreters, and the court reporter, without omitting to mention the security officers. Today we shall continue the cross-examination. Unless there are any points to be raised, let me ask the usher to be kind enough to bring in General Reinhardt.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, let me check first that you are hearing well the interpretation of what I am saying in your headset.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We have no technical problems, then. I turn now to Mr. Bourgon to give him the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Madam Judge. Good morning, Your Honour. Good morning, Mr. President. Before beginning the next part of my cross-examination, Mr. President, the Defence would like to offer its apologies because of the delay yesterday. We overstepped our time limit. Sometimes it's difficult to stop in the middle of a topic, but we will do our best not to allow that to happen again. The second point I wish to raise, Mr. President, that yesterday the Defence took efforts to provide the references of certain documents which were tendered, and I have them now and I should like the usher to assist us in distributing the sources of documents that were lacking yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber notes that for documents DH140, 139, 147 we are given the references and the numbers. Is this satisfactory for the Prosecution, Mr. Mundis?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. It is indeed satisfactory. I'm just wondering perhaps if this should somehow be marked and/or somehow attached to the record so that this document becomes part of the case file.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Registrar, let us give this document a number so that it can be added to the documents that have already been tendered. In this way, we can refer to this document when we are talking about Exhibits 139, 140, 150, and 145.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] DH151, that will be the exhibit number of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the document has been filed as Exhibit 151. Mr. Bourgon, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. As announced by the Defence yesterday, Mr. President, we are now going to move on to the implementation of the technical matters that we covered with the witness yesterday. The first part has to do with the responsibilities and duties of the commander, and we will focus on the role of a commander at the level of the corps, which will be followed by a legal issue section regarding the applicable law during 1993 in Bosnia, and then we will have some questions regarding the points he made in his report. We will then go on to the evaluation of the situation as seen by the witness during his studies of the large number of documents he was provided with. Finally, Mr. President, we will study with the witness the measures that may have -- that could have been taken by the commander, General Enver Hadzihasanovic, during his mission as commander of the 3rd Corps in Central Bosnia. Without further delay, Mr. President, I turn now to the witness to continue with my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yesterday, General, we -- we ended the day by referring to the reasonable commander, and my first question for you this morning, General, would be as follows: Would you agree with me that in determining the individual criminal responsibility of a commanding general of a corps, for the type of liability or the type of charges he is facing in this trial, namely, that he did not take the necessary and reasonable measures to either prevent or to suppress the actions of his subordinate, would you agree with me, General, that it is necessary in doing so to look at the situation and the context in which General Hadzihasanovic exercised his command?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Would you agree with me, General, that it is important actually to try and understand the position he was in and the many difficulties he faced which might have a bearing on either his ability to take some actions or the timing with which he took these actions?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If I mention to you, General, that the evaluation of these factors would include such things as the nature of the assignment or the mission that was given to General Hadzihasanovic, would that be a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only to some extent, sir, because the provisions of the law are independent from the situation. It might be that it might be delayed, but the provisions of the law as such remain, notwithstanding the situation, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. As we discussed yesterday, General, we mentioned that the law basically remained in force at all times.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: That the law was the left and right boundaries, but that within those boundaries the commander had to focus on the mission.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. No question about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: In terms of the nature of the mission General Hadzihasanovic was entrusted with, would you agree with me that if I try to qualify this mission, it was a mission which included the waging of war operations in a defensive mode in his own national territory facing two different enemies?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: In terms of the nature of the mission - moving on, once we have qualified it as being waging war on a national territory - the nature of the mission, in terms of the urgency of the military actions required in this context and the importance of taking some actions to succeed in the mission is a factor that might have affected either his ability at a given moment to take some actions.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Would you agree with me, General, that the resources that were available to the general would also be a very important criteria, and I'd like to qualify the resources in terms of, first, human resources. Maybe my question is not precise enough. Let me rephrase this, General. In terms of factors that would affect the exercise of command or have an impact on the exercise of command, would the resources available to the commanding general be a relevant factor?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a key factor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And when we say that resources is a key factor, if I speak about human resources, such as the number of soldiers he had at his disposal, the professionalism of the soldiers at his disposal, the training of the soldiers at his disposal, the preparation of the soldiers at his disposal, and the specialist qualifications of his soldiers, including both from a technical point of view and from a leadership point of view, would all of the above be important factors dealing with human resources that would have an impact on the exercise of command by General Hadzihasanovic?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Moving on, General, to materiel resources. And again, I'll try to give you a list, and I'll go slowly. Such things as money or the financial situation of the state, weapons, available ammunitions, transportation resources, communication equipment, infrastructures, including electricity, shelters, and accommodations, and what you may refer to as combat supplies; namely, food, water, fuel, or petroleum products, and medical supplies. Would the limited resources available falling in these categories be a definite factor which would impact on the exercise of command by General Hadzihasanovic?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: General, I would like to know if you are familiar with a World War II war crimes trial, that of the German General Rendulic.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Rendulic. I know about him, but I don't know about the trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'm sorry about the pronunciation, Rendulic. I'd like to give you a very quick overview of the situation he was in and follow on with a question as to what happened to him during this trial. General Rendulic was -- had to retreat over a very long territory of many hundreds of kilometres, and as part of this retreat he was under the impression that the Russian forces at his pursuit were closing in on him. Having done his assessment of the situation, he considered that it was necessary to prevent the enemy or the pursuing force, to get the resources from the land that he was retreating from in order to catch him. Would I be -- would it be fair to say that this can be referred to as the scorched earth policy?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And General Rendulic actually applied this policy of scorched earth and was actually accused for doing so following World War II. This was one of the charges he faced. There were other charges. In this specific case, General, the conclusion of the military court was as follows: They basically came to the conclusion that when the trial took place, the assessment that the court could do in the courtroom was that there was probably and most likely no need to do a scorched earth policy in the circumstances, but the Court concluded that when assessing the exercise of command by a general, it was necessary to look at what he saw when he was there and to fully consider all of the circumstances he was in in order to determine whether his decision-making was appropriate at the time. And for this reason, the Court found him not guilty of this charge. Would you comment on this case of General Rendulic.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: My first question, sir, is: What court was it? Was it a German military court or was it the court of the victory, of the winning forces? Because that makes a big difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: It was, General, the international -- it was an international military tribunal as Nuremberg, but it wasn't the Nuremberg trial.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And it was the High Command case.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. I think the -- the policy of torched ground was a very common policy in the Russian campaign on either side, and I don't know the exact conditions under which General Rendulic fought by that time, but I'm with you; one has to consider the overall situation as he has seen them -- has seen them and as he evaluated it at the time when he was retreating over that stretch of country.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And would you agree with me, General, that all of the circumstances at the time that would affect or that may have had an impact on his decision-making would also be relevant in order to assess the exercise of his command?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If I mention to you a number of issues, would you -- I would appreciate it if you could confirm whether these issues could have an impact on the exercise of command by a commanding general of a corps: Issues such as enemy forces.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And I would include, in terms of enemy forces, the strength of the enemy forces, the armament of the enemy forces, the doctrine, the war-fighting doctrine of the enemy forces, as well as any crimes committed by enemy forces.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would go with you until the last part, because I think the crimes have to be considered. But they are not a real effect on your own operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, General, if I mention to you that in the context of a war crimes committed by the enemy forces will indeed have a very serious impact on the morale of your own soldiers and on the measures that you may need to even better control these soldiers and ensure that they abide by the law --

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: -- because the enemy is violating the law.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. This is a key problem, then, for the commander, that his own soldiers don't do the same things as the enemy has done to their own forces, and I think this is a key question for the discipline and morale of your own forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: We've mentioned already, General, issues such as organisation of the army and professionalism of the army. Would you qualify the impact of those on the exercise of command.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very much so.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Could you elaborate as to how it could impact on the exercise of command.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you have forces not qualified adequately for the mission given to them, they will fail. If you have enemy forces better qualified, better prepared for the mission, they will succeed. And the key thing of operations is to win the operations and not to lose the operations, so the better your soldiers are qualified, trained, and by being better trained and qualified, their morale booster is higher up than the ones of poor soldiers. The bigger are the chances that you will prevail in this campaign.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Moving on to a different type of factor, that of the civilian population and the treatment of the civilian population by enemy forces. Would that also be a very important factor that could affect the morale and the fighting ability of your own troops, given that the civilian population is of the same ethnic and national background?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's always very difficult to fight while the civilian population is still in place, but what you just said will have a detrimental effect on your own soldier. And I come back to what we discussed just before. Even so -- just because of that, your countermeasures on stabilising the morale are even more important.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if I mention to you the presence of thousands of refugees in the area of responsibility of the commander, would that be a critical factor? And if so, why?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It will be a critical factor, because it hampers your freedom of movement; it hampers your possibility to use your weapon systems the way you would like to use them, because you don't want to kill your own population. So you're much more restricted than operating in an area where no civil population is; therefore, normally in a case like this you try to clear up the area before you go in war.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: General, another issue I would like to raise with you is should in the case of waging war on your own national territory the law enforcement agencies still be operating - namely, I'm talking about the civil law enforcement agencies - the effectiveness of these agencies in dealing with common crimes, would that be a factor that could affect the exercise of command?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very much so, because if they don't do it, you have to do it with your own scarce resources. And I would always appreciate to still have those civil authorities taking care of people who are committing crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And another issue, General, is that of the presence in the area of international observers, non-governmental organisations, international organisations such as the International Committee of the Red Cross, as well as the presence of medias, would that have an impact on the exercise of command?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would, because you have to consider that what everything you're doing is like doing it in the glasshouse. You're being watched and observed from every side in a very critical way, and you have to make sure that the things you're doing will not have a detrimental effect in this International Community as long as people are there to help you, and the NGOs and IOs and other organisations you were talking about, including all these international organisations were there for the benefit of -- of the people living in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And talking about the presence of such organisations and having a specific question which applies to this case, if we are talking about the presence of the United Nations Protection Force, UNPROFOR, would that be a fair statement that it would be normal and even more than normal, but it would be the way to go for a commanding general to fully cooperate with UNPROFOR while at the same time ensuring that they do not get access to your plans so that they do not become an impeding factor on any operations you want to lead?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with you. UNPROFOR was there not to wage war but to provide internal security. And we all remember how difficult it was and that the outcome was a very detrimental one. But as a commander, you would never jeopardise your plans by talking about those plans with UNPROFOR, which are not working with you militarily. They were working only in supporting on a very different level.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But nevertheless, given the mandate of UNPROFOR, it would be a good thing for the commander to cooperate with UNPROFOR within the scope of their mandate.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If I mention to you the geography of the terrain, is that an important factor for the commander?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very much so.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If I may ask you, General, to quickly just stand up and take a look at the model in front of you. I'm not sure that you are able to see the model.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, at this stage I should like to ask the witness, without having him to answer any question, to walk around and look and see whether he can recognise the model as representing the area that he visited with the German troops; that is, Visoko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, General, could you please walk around the model and take your time to look at the places. And we must point out that this model was prepared -- this model was prepared by the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. My first question to you, having taken a look at the model, is: On the basis of your previous presence in this area, do you recognise any of the area?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. And this is not only that I have been there as a soldier. I've been there during the Olympic Games in Sarajevo, and I skied the Bijelasnjica and some other areas, so I think I'm rather familiar with the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. How would you qualify the model you have just taken a look at and the conditions of the -- sorry, the geography of the terrain, in terms of waging a war in this type of context?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a very difficult terrain because it's what we call in our military jargon a broken terrain, hilly, wooded terrain, a lot of villages where -- a lot of separated areas, valleys and high ground, not an area very favourable for mechanised forces. It's very favourable more or less for dismounted infantry supported. It would be ideal to fight here with helicopter and -- and very light mobile forces. I think it's -- it's a very difficult terrain to continue the cohesion of the operations within it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. If I mention to you another factor that would impede on the ability of the commander to exercise his duties as being the proximity of the FEBA. Now, FEBA, I may be late with the terms I use but FEBA being the forward edge of the battle area. Would that be an important factor for the commander?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But to just caution it a little bit, I think it's difficult to talk about one FEBA like a consolidated line throughout the area. There were also pockets of operations, not so much connected with each other. So it's not the normal way that you would fight with the mechanised or a modern corps operations because -- because of the terrain and also because of the difference, having to fight two enemies at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if I change my term "FEBA" for the proximity of the war fighting real action to the headquarters of the commander, would that be an important factor?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's an important factor because it also somehow alleviates the problem of communication, because the closer you are to the front, the easier it gets to -- to close this distance by other means than -- than normal means you might have. You don't need satellites to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if the headquarters of the commanding general in this case was located in Zenica -- you are able to confirm this from the documents?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that Zenica was being shelled on a regular basis, would that have an impact on the work going on in the 3rd Corps command headquarters?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure. Once you're shelled, your efficiency goes down immediately, because you have to take cover and -- and try to survive, rather than to continue to operate.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And one last question, because you mentioned the issue of communications. Would you agree with me, General, that terrain such as is depicted by this model in Central Bosnia with, as you mentioned, woods, mountains, hilly, would that be more or less difficult to communicate?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's much more difficult to communicate, because you don't have the -- the sight of line from one radio to the next one, which you normally need to have in radio communications, so you have to work with a lot of different ways, and I think this is one of the reasons, as far as I saw it myself, that most of the forces tried to -- to work with Motorola.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And one last objective question, if I may describe my questions as such, in terms of factors which may impede the work of the commander: How about the size of his area, the area of operations of the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's been a large area for the corps. I think it was appropriate also for a corps. The whole Bosnian area for Bosnia-Herzegovina was split up in five different zones, with five different corps. And I think the area for the 3rd Corps was somehow appropriate to the forces the commander had at his availability.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I have a few specific questions dealing with the facts or the documents that you have already seen, in respect of factors which could impede the ability of the commander to exercise his command. And the first one I'd like to mention to you: Did you or were you able to conclude from the documents which were shown to you that there was a very strong use of propaganda by the HVO forces?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there was a strong use of propaganda of all forces involved in these operations, but I could not -- I could not say I would see a stronger involvement of propaganda -- at least, it didn't show up for me through looking through the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if you would have concluded differently -- now, this is a hypothetical question, given your answer to the previous question. If the propaganda actions of the HVO would have been very significant and even that if the HVO had wanted to alarm its own population and create panic in its own population, would that have an impact on the exercise of command of General Hadzihasanovic?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It might have, but I think as soon as you have population in an area of combat, the population is terrorised. No matter whether you have additional propaganda assets, the population would use in the way you just described it, to react in the way you just described it, because for them sometimes it's almost impossible to realise who were shooting against them, from what side.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: The next issue I'd like to cover, General, is that of roads. How important are roads for the commanding general of a corps?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: The more mechanised you are, the more important are the status of roads. The less mechanised you are, the less important they get. But one thing is absolutely clear: Behind every kind of forces you need supply logistic forces, and logistic forces need roads because they negotiate heavy equipment and heavy bulky loads, and if they don't have roads, they cannot deliver what they are supposed to deliver for the sake of the operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And would it be a fair statement, General, to say that as soon as the ability to use a road that is required is reduced or even completely blocked, that the commanding general will focus his attention in finding a road or building a road or ensuring that what this road was used for, find a way to do that?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that this is indeed a very important endeavour for the commanding general of a corps.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If I mention to you, General, the political nature or the political moves of the enemy forces generally - and I'll move then into more specifics - would that have an impact on the ability of a commander to exercise his command?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, every move of the enemy will have an impact on his capabilities. I think that's what the enemy is all about. It's -- it's not only the military; it's also the political and the psychological, and as we just said before, the propaganda effects which will have impact on your own forces and on your own capabilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, General, if I give you a specific case whereas General Hadzihasanovic assumed his command in November of 1992, are you able to confirm that?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if I mention to you that prior to General Hadzihasanovic exercising or assuming his command there was a case in which a town was given an ultimatum to lay down their weapons and surrender to the HVO, and indeed did so, would this factor have an impact on the assessment of the situation and the way General Hadzihasanovic would conduct his operations after assuming command?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that particular case, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: When a commanding general loses a village in his area to the enemy, what are the consequences for the general?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Because I think one might over-exaggerate now the loss of a village. There was many, many villages, also villages which have been taken back and forth. I think it really depends what kind of village, whether it was in a strategic area or not. Just the loss of one village is one case which happens in the operations which you have to reckon, and therefore I'm not -- I'm not able to give you a qualified answer on your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. You mentioned yesterday that in Germany the focus was placed on using all resources of the state should a situation like that in Bosnia would arise [sic].

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Would I be right in saying that the commanding general losing a village - and of course, it all depends on where the village is and the size of the village - but would I be right in saying that by losing a village he also loses the resources that he could get from this village as well as any assistance he might get from the civil or lawful civil authorities that were working in this village?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is obvious.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: We've mentioned, General, the issue of refugees, and your answer dealt with population movements. Whoever causes population movements in the area, would it be fair to say that population movements will impede the decision-making of the commanding general because he may have to alter his plans of operations he was intending to lead?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very much so.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: What I would like to do at this time, General, is simply to ask you whether you were in a position from the documents that you had and that you had a look at to assess the forces or the organisation of the 3rd Corps and the troops that were available to General Hadzihasanovic.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there is a document in which the forces available to him are laid down in -- in the organisation order of the 3rd Corps. But as I also already mentioned yesterday or the day before yesterday, the -- the terms for an organisation very often don't match our terms. So a brigade doesn't say that every brigade -- the term "brigade" doesn't say that every brigade has the same size, because very often they were different in size. Also, battalions were not always in the same size. So yes, the overall organisation, I think, has been laid down, and I also read a number which General Hadzihasanovic has mentioned at the beginning when he took over his corps, and that this then increased over the time, but the number I read was in a document which I'm not allowed to quote; therefore, I don't know the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: General, I would like to show you a document which I prepared myself from the documents that were at your disposal, and I would like you to take a look at this document and to tell me whether the information included in this document, one, could be derived from the information that was given to you; and, two, whether it would be a fair assessment at the troops that were at the disposal of General Hadzihasanovic [sic].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'm just wondering -- I see what might be one reference to an ERN number on this document. I'm wondering if that -- if my learned colleague can inform us whether that ERN number reflects the totality of the source of the information on this document which he has prepared or if there are other documents from which he also compiled this information, and if we could have the ERN numbers or any other identifying numbers with respect to all the documents used in preparing this current document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. The references that my learned friend is referring to only refer to the percentage indicated, the percentage of soldiers present within the 3rd Corps. This figure should be compared with the theoretical effective authorised by the government for the corps. Therefore, the reference L0098218 is a reference to a document dated -- I don't know, either the 23rd of July or the 1st of August, 1993. And in this document, mention is made of all the troops of each unit and the percentage of existing soldiers in each of those units compared to the total effective, as well as total percentage of soldiers within the 3rd Corps as compared to the number according to formation. The rest of the information comes from a host of documents, and that is why I'm asking the witness, that is, General Reinhardt, whether the document that I myself prepared could be an illustration of the troops available to General Hadzihasanovic. I have no intention of spending a lot of time on this matter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I see that, I think this is a -- a very good compilation. I basically based my information on the Supreme Command Staff of the Armed Forces, Sarajevo, 9 November, the initial order on the composition of the corps, knowing as I said that the corps has changed over time, which you can deduct from the sources from the documents available to me. But I think the overall strength and the overall composition as you have laid it down here in this chart is the one that I would agree to.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General. There's another document that I would like to show you at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As the Chamber will not have questions for the witness on the basis of this document, you mentioned Municipal Defensive Staff Zenica. Could you tell us what it means, "1 Municipal Defensive Staff (Zenica)." The municipal defensive staff of Zenica. Is this a military or civilian structure that you have integrated within the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that the best thing would be to ask the witness to explain what he believes this means. Could he define for us the Municipal Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [In English] [Previous translation continues] ... are you able to explain what was the Municipal Staff of Zenica? And we see that there are other Municipal Staffs. For example, I refer to Operational Group East, and we see there are five municipal defence staffs, one in Visoko, one in Vares, one in Kiseljak, one in Kresevo, and one in Fojnica. Are you able to explain to the Trial Chamber what was or what were these municipal defence staffs?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not quite sure whether I'm capable of doing that, because I never looked into that in detail. But, sir, the corps was built up of territorial forces, and the municipal defensive staff were elements of those territorial forces prepared for the defence of the country, and those were elements of the military, also of the civil authorities in the area, which were capable of defending their area of responsibility, and they were then incorporated into the corps forces operating in that area for the unity -- for the sake of the unity of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: General, moving on or pursuing in this area, because indeed it is a very -- it is a very important issue, were you able to conclude on the basis of the documents that were given to you how the evolution of the creation of the 3rd Corps proceeded from the end of 1992 until the 1st November 1993? And I mean exactly the relationship between what you have referred to as Territorial Defence and the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the Territorial Defence was the basic organisation in the area, which was then taken over by the 3rd Corps and the other corps, included as the basis of the forces for those corps, and therefore the Territorial Defence as such did not prevail; it became a part of the -- of the corps forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And were you able to conclude from the documents given to you that at some point in time during the year of 1993 initially the district staff, which was the element above the municipal defence staff, disappeared and was amalgamated into the 3rd Corps, and this was a procedure that evolved from the beginning until the end, in terms of creating military structure from the corps and step by step amalgamating this structure to create a more effective chain of command and control within the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: You just explained it in a better way than I tried to do it before.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would like to tender this document into evidence. Could we have an exhibit number for the document, since the witness has recognised that it is an accurate reflection of the information contained in the document that he's been shown.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, with regard to this document presented by the Defence, it goes to prove that the 3rd Corps in fact only had 73 per cent of the full strength, 32.000 men; whereas, 43.000 men constitute the full strength, and there is a general scheme, a general representation of how the 3rd Corps was constituted. It mentions four independent brigades; the 7th Mountain Brigade, the 301st Brigade, the 309th Brigade, and then it mentions five operational groups which were deployed. The document also refers to the Municipal Staff, which seems linked to places such as Kakanj, Busovaca, Visoko, et cetera. What is the Prosecution's position as far as this document is concerned?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I note from the document on the upper left, immediately following "3rd ABiH Corps" in parentheses it indicates "end of June 1993." If, in fact, Mr. Bourgon is prepared to confirm that this picture portrays the 3rd Corps at the end of June 1993, we certainly have no objection to this document being admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Prosecution says that this document reflects the situation at the end of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. My -- the Prosecution's comment, saying that this concerns the 3rd Corps at the end of June 1993, with regard to this comment we can say that it was certainly the situation in June 1993. But to answer the question more precisely, I would have to have a look at the document or the date, because the information concerning the numbers contained in the document come from one of the two sources. Unfortunately, I can't remember whether it's the document dated August or the 23rd of June. So with your leave, Mr. President, I could check that during the break, and then respond in more precise terms to the comments my colleague made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We will give this document a number after the pause. For the moment, it will be on standby.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [In English] [Previous translation continues] ... and that is this document is a summary of a commanding general's responsibility. In fact, it is a summary of a commandant's responsibilities. And I would like you to take a look at this document and confirm that this is what on a daily basis a commander does and that these are a fair representation of what a commander does on a day-to-day basis.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a very new document. To provide a vision --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: This is a document I put together myself, General.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: To provide a vision, because the "vision" is the new term. If you don't have a vision, you're nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The witness has told the Defence that "to provide a vision" is a recent concept, which was probably not in force in 1993. Would the witness confirm that the idea of providing a vision was one that did not exist in 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would call it to provide a guidance, rather than a vision, and that's what he's doing. He gives the main guidance, the mental and the operational guidance, and I think that's what you want to say here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: General, I would ask you to maybe if you have something to write, to cross out any information with which you do not agree in this document and to sign this document, the aim being to have a document that portrays daily occupations, responsibilities, and actions of a commander, and more specifically a corps commander, in 1993.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: How much time do you give me?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If you need time, I better withdraw the document. It's up to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I ask a question, Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just don't understand what you would like to say by the -- the second bullet from -- from below, "to create a sense of involvement in decision-making and share commitment." I don't understand what it means, "To create a sense of involvement in decision-making."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: What is meant when I wrote this, because it is taken from one of the references I read, and it was explained in that reference as meaning to have -- to feel that the leadership is part of the same mission and that they shared the same goals in their decision-making process.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Okay, I understand. I just wanted to be enlightened. Yes, sir. I haven't scratched anything out.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Would you please, General, initial this document.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would like to tender this document into evidence, and I would like an exhibit number for the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, there is one question I would like to ask you in order to clarify something. You have proved that the contents of this document -- you have confirmed the contents of the document. But as a former member of the military, is there anything that is missing in the document? And I'm thinking of the relations to the civilian authorities that must have occupied the corps commander on a 24-hour basis, the relations to the media, et cetera. In your opinion, is this a complete document or are there some elements that are missing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, these are the major missions of the commander, and it incorporates also the cooperation with the media, information operations, taking care of refugees and all these things. But this is a kind of his decision-making in leadership directive, which he will encompass for what he is supposed to do, so I would not like to enumerate all these additional things which -- which fall under his decision-making process. I think this is a part of his command responsibility, as I see this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Mundis, the Defence would like this document to be admitted into evidence. It has been identified by the witness, who doesn't criticise it. What is the Prosecution's position with regard to the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution is not quite sure of the purpose of the document, particularly in light of the witness's question to Your Honour that this is part of the command responsibility. But perhaps that goes more to weight. So we have no objection as to the admissibility of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Registrar, could we have an exhibit number for the document, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] DH152 will be the exhibit number of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can continue, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [In English] To add to the question you have just answered, General, would I be right in saying that it would almost be an impossible task to enumerate everything that a commander may be asked to do in the exercise of his command because it all depends very much on the circumstances and the nature of his mission?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I was, I think, rather well prepared to command the corps, but once I have done this, I had to do things I never have dreamed of before, that I would ever be forced to do this. So you really have to have an ad hoc decision whether this encompasses this or not. But I think, again, it's in the daily routine that you have to be flexible enough to deal with all the things which you have to deal with.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, General, based on your experience, having been a commander for most of your life - and I think we -- it's fair to say that it is for most of your life you have been commanding troops - would it be fair to say that the exercise of command is very difficult, is complex, and that in fact it can be referred to as being a calling?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sometimes I don't know what -- whether the -- whether "calling" is the proper term, because I don't -- I'm not familiar with this term. But I tell you very often it's -- it's a very tough burden which you sometimes like to -- to skip and escape.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if I provide you with an example where commanders are faced with a decision sometimes where they may have to sacrifice the lives of their own troops knowingly for the success of an operation, would I be right in saying that a decision such as this one - and I think very few people face such a high threshold of decision-making - but my issue is this type of decision, is that what we refer to when we speak about the burden of command?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And would I be right in saying that because it is a very detailed profession and that there are many components to the exercise of command, that it is also very much an individual matter and a subjective matter in that two commanders placed in the same situation may react differently and yet both be effective and good commanders?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I move on now, General, to my next part of my cross-examination, which deals with the law applicable to the operations of the 3rd Corps in Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1993. And my first question, General, is whether from reading the documents that you have been given, whether you were able to conclude or to note - because not a conclusion but to see - that because General Hadzihasanovic was waging war on his own national territory, that the civil authorities were still in operation in 1993.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that there was a relationship between the various civil organisations, in terms of the fact that they had duties towards the military.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I refer to one specific document, which is the decree law or decree -- sorry, I will get close to the microphone -- the decree with the force of law on defence. And this document was given to you. And I'm looking at the number. All I have is the ERN number. But I will try to give you a better number.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is this -- sir, is this the same, the decree with the powers of law of the armed forces? Because sometimes the translations are mixed up.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I don't think it is the same document, General. This is the decree with the force of law on defence.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And this document covers the relationship between the various civil organisations and quickly mentions the army but also determines that there were responsibilities of the civil organisations towards the army. I'm sorry, General, it's just been indicated to me that maybe you did not receive this document.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not I am aware of; therefore, I asked this question. Because it's almost identical in -- in the wording, but I think I haven't seen this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: This document actually, General, is the basic document that determines the relationship between --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bourgon, so that the Trial Chamber can find its bearings, could you indicate the number of this document of the Prosecution's -- the Prosecution number or the PT number, because we have a table here and then a list of documents that were provided to the witness should be referred to too.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. This document wasn't provided to the witness, according to my notes. It's my mistake. I worked on this document in order to prepare my cross-examination. I was certain that he had received it, since it's really an essential document. We'll check this during the break, Mr. President. We'll check the exact number of the document to see whether the Prosecution has put forth this document and to see whether it's been admitted, because all the governmental documents are ones that the Defence has agreed to have admitted, and unfortunately, Mr. President, I believe that this document hasn't even been tendered by the Prosecution. But I'll check this during the break in order to avoid any problems. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [In English] General, I move on with my questions. I see we have ten minutes before the technical break. What I wanted to go over with you, in terms of legal regime applicable: You are in fact able to confirm that the civil authorities, civil organisations, were indeed operating --

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: -- in Central Bosnia at the same time as the 3rd Corps was conducting its operations.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Are you able to also confirm that the mission General Hadzihasanovic was entrusted with and that his responsibilities were solely limited to military matters and that things such as civil -- or law enforcement were not his responsibility?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Were you able to confirm that an organisation referred to in a documents as MUP, M-U-P, was operating in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Were you able to confirm that civil security organisations were also operating in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I read about civil security organisations passim in the written statements of some witnesses, but I didn't look into much detail in this one, because I was not interested in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Did you -- or were you able to confirm from the documents given to you that there was a relationship or cooperation being exercised between the 3rd Corps and civil organisations, and more specifically the MUP?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this is a clear necessity that they had worked together, being in the same area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But from the documents that you have read, were you able to confirm that indeed they were cooperating?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Were you able to confirm from the documents you've read that the justice or judicial system was also still in operation?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about the district military courts. I don't know about the other courts. But there must have been a justice system, because the corps commander ordered the brigade commander to provide for legal assistance on their level from the population, in which they -- they operated. So there must have been this organisation still working.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, General, given that you were asked to give an opinion on any measures taken by the commander of the 3rd Corps, did you find it necessary to determine what those relationships were between civil organisations - namely, the MUP, the judicial system, and the 3rd Corps - in order to determine whether such measures had or had not been taken by General Hadzihasanovic?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only realised, sir, that there was a cooperation, but I don't know about the individual measures through which this cooperation took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But as you mentioned yesterday, General, if, to take the example of the German Army, once a commander is aware of a violation of the law, no matter what type of violation, he must see to it that something is done about the violation -- Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and in some cases he will have the power to deal with it personally; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that in other cases he will have to refer the matter to the courts.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's absolutely true.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if I take this situation, is that the type of system that you saw from the documents that were given to you as being applicable in Central Bosnia in 1993?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: You mentioned that there were no, in Germany, disciplinary -- military -- sorry, district military courts.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Did you notice from the documents given to you that district military courts were created only in times of war?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that district military prosecutor's offices were also only created in times of war?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that the district military prosecutor's office had responsibilities to investigate cases of violations and to bring the matter to the district military courts?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that to do this the district military prosecutor could obtain information from various sources, including but not limited to the 3rd Corps and its subordinate units?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that the -- if I look at the handling of violations in Central Bosnia in 1993, would I be right in saying that this system worked on the following levels: First, there were disciplinary offences which could be divided in two, in terms of disciplinary fault and disciplinary violation, and that those would be handled inside the military?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that these would usually be dealt with by a military disciplinary court, which was inside the military.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that this military disciplinary court had in itself some levels where some matters could be dealt with by an assessor or a judge sitting alone; in some matters two judges, called a council; and in other matters by three assessors or judges sitting together?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that the offences, the disciplinary offences, there could be cases where an offence would qualify both as a violation or a disciplinary violation, the more serious type, and a criminal act in accordance with normal criminal system of the state?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that in such cases it would be possible, according to Article 6 of the Manual on Military Discipline, that a normal criminal act could be treated and handled as a disciplinary violation.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Nevertheless, you mentioned in your report, and you will agree with me that pursuant to Article 5 for a perpetrated criminal act or misdemeanour military persons were responsible to the normal criminal law system of the state?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: The second level of court --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think that I will stop here, because I have another ten minutes for the witness. I will continue after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It's now half past 10.00. We will resume at five to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bourgon, you have the floor again.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. At this stage, Mr. President, I should like to clear up two questions that were raised during the first part of this morning's hearing. First of all, Mr. President, the question of the diagram illustrating the 3rd Corps and the forces under the responsibility of General Hadzihasanovic. Having consulted the files and the documents, I am able to confirm that the numbers regarding the number of troops date from the end of June 1993; whereas, the composition of the units dates from the end of August. As I had information coming from two documents, I'm able to say that the figures come back from the -- date from the end of June 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, the Defence has explained that June is the date when the number of soldiers was registered and the composition of the 3rd Corps was as it existed at the end of August. That is what the Defence is telling us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And Mr. Bourgon for that information. In light of this clarification, Mr. President, the Prosecution has no objection if the Defence still would like to tender that document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Registrar, will you give us an exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It will be DH153.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Regarding the second question raised at the end of the hearing before the break, it has to do with the document entitled, "Decree with the force of law on defence." It is a document which is already on the file. This document has the number DH29. It is Exhibit Number DH29. It was a document tendered by the Defence during the cross-examination of a witness. We could also add, Mr. President, that this document was provided to us by the Prosecution together with all the -- all the other documents that were disclosed to us by the Prosecution prior to the beginning of trial. Finally, Mr. President, we can also confirm that this document was not given to the witness who is currently before the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Chamber will have a look at that document, DH29. DH29 is in B/C/S. Is there a English translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have the translation with me. It's a translation given to us, we believe, by the Prosecution, as it has a translation code.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the registrar see whether we have DH29/E.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, we do have the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please continue, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [In English] General, following this technical break, I would like to move on and I have just a few additional questions on the judicial system and the way violations of the law could be addressed by the commander of the 3rd Corps. And before the break, we -- you confirmed that you were aware of the disciplinary regime and of the military disciplinary court which was within the military.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And we were now looking at the, on one hand, the district military prosecutor's office, as well as the district military court. And you confirmed from your reading of the documents the existence of both of these bodies.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And we confirmed that there were responsibilities which were entrusted to the district military prosecutor, in terms of investigating offences and making sure that he would bring the matter up to the district military court.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And we also confirmed that information to do this could be provided to the district military prosecutor from a variety of sources, including the 3rd Corps, as well as its subordinate units.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: You will agree with me, General, that both the district military prosecutor's office and the district military court are agencies or organisations - I'm not sure exactly what term to use - that are external to the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: As would be the system in Germany that you are used to, but they bear the name "military" because they were created in times of war. And that once an issue, or once a complaint has been brought to the attention of the district military prosecutor by the 3rd Corps - meaning whether it is the commander of the 3rd Corps or one of its subordinate units - then that for all intents and purposes the duty of the commander has been accomplished.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Nevertheless, you mention in your report that should the commander feel that not enough is being done by this district military prosecutor or the district military court, that it would be his duty to do something about it.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you confirm in your report that this is exactly what General Hadzihasanovic did by bringing the matter to the attention of the court.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sorry, did bring this to the attention of the supreme headquarters.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of the supreme headquarters. That he was not very happy with the situation, the things were dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And he did complain that this was having an impact because it wasn't going fast enough.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, the -- I mentioned before the break that there were three levels of justice. Would I be right in saying that the third level of justice was the special military court?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that the special military court could be created by a military commander within the military upon being authorised to do so by his superior?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that this would only take place in very specific circumstances, meaning that it would be during the state of war such a special military court may be established, but the conditions was if in the assessment of the commander of a regiment or a brigade, the conditions for conducting criminal proceedings before a competent district military court either did not exist or were difficult and that the combat situation required that proceedings be conducted without delay.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you are able to confirm from the documents that were given to you that General Hadzihasanovic did create or authorise his subordinate units to create special military courts.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: He authorised them, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that in fact subordinate units did create special military courts.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I did not read about the establishment of a special military court. I don't remember this.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I will refer later to a document, rather than wasting time --

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: -- on showing you a document. I will refer to a document later to confirm this issue. You are able to confirm, however, General, that the type of offences for which this special military court would be used were usually combat-related offences, such as surrender to the enemy, joining the enemy forces, or undermining morale in combat.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that the commander who established a court would also be the one who would appoint the judges and there would be five members to this court.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you are able to confirm that the only possible sentence that this court could give was a death sentence.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that if the district -- if the special military court, even if it found someone guilty, if it disagreed or did not wish to impose the death penalty, that it would then be -- have to refer the matter to the district military prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that if the death penalty or the death sentence was pronounced, it could be carried out on the order of the unit of the commander who had awarded the death sentence.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that this would be done by a firing squad.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: You would agree with me, General, that looking at the law applicable to the operations of the 3rd Corps, that there was indeed, first on one hand, working civil organisations who were responsible for law enforcement?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that as far as military issues are concerned, or military violations, there was a three-level system, starting from disciplinary violations, moving on to criminal acts or misdemeanour, and another different type, which were the offences that the special military court could deal with.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that General Hadzihasanovic did take some steps for this system to operate at the three levels.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If I may -- if I may continue on one matter dealing with the legal regime applicable. And that is just to confirm, because there may have been some confusion. If in your view -- I would like to ask you to give me your views as to whether General Hadzihasanovic would have been responsible for violations of the law committed by civilians; for example, in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And would I be right in saying that General Hadzihasanovic was not responsible for violations which would be committed, to give another example, by members of BritBat?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that he would not be responsible either for violations committed by international observers or members of the European Community Monitoring Mission?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that he would not be responsible for violations committed by the MUP --

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: -- or by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: By the?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: HVO.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: The enemy. Or by the Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So, in fact, you would agree with me that General Hadzihasanovic, his responsibility with respect to handling violations was limited to soldiers or members of the military who were under his effective command and control.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I now move on, General, to the next part of my cross-examination, dealing with the military situation of the 3rd Corps in specific terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, at this stage the Defence, in order to save time, would like to resort to a hypothetical case. We would like to show the witness a list of facts relating to the situation in which the 3rd Corps found itself and within which the command of the 3rd Corps operated during the period covered by the indictment, as well as on the dates which are relevant from the standpoint of the indictment. We would thus like to submit these facts. We will not be tendering any documents. We would only like to review these facts with the witness as an imaginary case, a hypothetical case. So the Defence would like to obtain from this witness his opinion regarding facts, and later on we will try to prove this to the Chamber but we will first submit these facts to the witness in order to fully take advantage of his presence and his capacity as an expert witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber would like to hear the opinion of the Prosecution. But in order to summarise the procedure you are suggesting, you're going to show to the military expert, who is in front of us, taking into account his knowledge of the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina, of military rules, the constitution of the 3rd Corps and all the other facts that he has command of, you are going to ask him his opinion about some fictitious facts and you are going to ask him questions on the basis of a hypothetical case, this is a hypothetical case but which could be real at the same time, for the witness to give his opinion and interpretation of the situation as you will present it to him. What is the position of the Prosecution regarding this suggested procedure which would allow an expert to give his opinion regarding different possible scenarios or facts which may have or could have occurred? What is your position, Mr. Mundis?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The Defence discussed this with the Prosecution prior to this morning's hearing. My understanding from Mr. Bourgon was that this was largely going to be discussion relating to the map or maps that are behind the witness. In principle, Mr. President, and in light of the jurisprudence of this Tribunal with respect to expert witnesses, the Prosecution does not object to hypothetical situations being put to the witness, again with the understanding that the questions are clear to the witness that they are hypothetical questions and may or may not stem from the actual facts of this case or the evidence which is before this Trial Chamber.
