So as long as everyone is aware of -- of the procedure that's being used, the Prosecution has no objection to this process being used with the expert witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understand, these questions could be posed within the framework of an officer's training course in a war college. You show them facts and ask them to assess them. So, Mr. Bourgon, as there are no objections, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To be a little bit more precise, to avoid all confusion, what we would like to ask the witness is that he has already had opportunity to review a number of documents he was provided with by the Prosecution, and he formed an opinion based on the documents he had access to. What we would like to do with the expert witness is to give him a series of additional facts in written form and to ask him if adding these facts to those he was aware of, what would have been your opinion regarding two or three particular matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to submit the series of facts to the witness, and I would like to ask Mr. Usher to be kind enough to distribute these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [In English] General Reinhardt, you have been provided by the Prosecution with a series of facts, a series of documents, and you have been asked to reply or to provide your opinion on the basis of these documents.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: What I would like to ask of you at this time on a hypothetical basis is to look at the facts that are on this document, and as you look at these facts, to do the mental exercise of adding these facts to your own knowledge that you have made to this point, and then I will ask you one or two questions on the basis of the sum of all the facts, only with the caveat, of course, that the facts that you are provided with by the Defence today are facts that are at this stage hypothetical. Do you understand the procedure that I would like to follow with you?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure, but I'll try. Because I -- I'm not quite sure whether the things which I see here are all hypothetical, but okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: To make myself a bit more clear, these are facts and everyone in the courtroom will be well aware that these are facts that the Defence will endeavour to prove at some point during this trial --

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: -- thus, when we do so, validating your opinion. So there is no surprise, in terms of the -- for the Prosecution, in terms of the procedure being used. And basically what we could have done instead is to show you one document for each of these facts or to go with -- and some kind of evidence. But for now, we simply wish you to look at these facts in order to save time and then it will be our own burden to do that. But your role today is to provide an opinion, and to save time we'd like you to confirm -- to provide your opinion on the facts that you have been made aware of plus these ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, may I proceed? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [In English] So I will proceed -- I will proceed, General, to go quickly with you over these facts one by one.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And there are 40-some of these facts. The first ones relate to the political situation. So I would say that this would be a hypothetical situation that: "On 6 April 1992 Bosnia-Herzegovina was recognised as an independent state by the European Union and the United States; that on the same day it proclaimed its independence and that it was attacked by JNA and Bosnian Serb forces. The Serb forces occupied the majority of the Bosnian territory." I will speak a bit slower to ensure the translators have the time to catch up with me. "On the 2nd of May, 1992, the capital of Bosnia, Sarajevo, was attacked and put under siege, and there was a blockage of state organs, economic, industrial, as well as military resources." "On 9 January 1992, the SDS proclaimed the Republic of the Serbian People with the aspiration of integrating it into the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia." "On 12 May 1992, the Bosnian Serb Assembly voted to create the Army of the Serbian Republic and effectively transforming the JNA units remaining in Bosnia into commands of the new army. On the same day the Constitutional Court of Bosnia declared that these decisions taken by the Republic of the Serbian People were illegal." Moving on to the next page: "On 18 November, the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna proclaimed its existence and claimed to be a separate or distinct 'political, cultural, economic, and territorial whole' in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Its purposes included the establishment of closer ties with Croatia, as evidenced by the HZ HB's use of the Croatian currency and the Croatian language. These aspirations were supported by Croatia, which granted Croatian citizenship to Bosnian Croats." General, are we moving together on this, or am I going too fast or --

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: -- are you able to follow?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's all right, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Moving on: "On the 18th of November, the HZHB was founded with the intention that it should secede from Bosnia and Herzegovina and with a view to unification with Croatia." "On the 8th of April, 1992, the Presidency of the HZHB at an emergency session issued a decision establishing the HVO as the 'supreme defence body of the Croatian people' in HZ HB." General, before we move on, are we -- are you familiar with the terms that we are employing so far in these facts?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: General, I would ask also that you disregard any mention that is in the column to the right of the document which appear in this instance by mistake and should not have been there.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: "On the 10th of April, 1992, Mate Boban decreed that the Bosnian Territorial Defence, which had been created the day before, was illegal on HZHB territory."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My colleague has some comments he would like to make, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'm wondering if I might briefly address the Trial Chamber in the absence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Presiding Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Mundis, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'm actually hesitant to get to my feet, but the Prosecution is a bit concerned with the procedure used for a number of reasons. First of all, the notion of hypothetical facts, as the Prosecution understands it, might be slightly different from the use of that term or that concept by the Defence. The facts that they are putting to the witness, there's actually at least two different categories of these facts. The first kind of set of facts that we have here are facts which are actually in evidence and are before the Trial Chamber as reflected in the source column, where the Defence either cites to "ADM," which I take to be an admission by the Prosecution and the Defence, or an exhibit number. Consequently, Mr. President, those are not, the Prosecution would submit, hypotheticals. They are clearly facts which are in evidence. With respect to some of the other facts that are set forth, those facts may or may not be true, and I haven't had the chance to thoroughly go through this document, having just received it. Many of these facts, however, at first glance appear to be facts which one or the other party submitted to the other in terms of pre-trial admissions, which the parties did not agree to based on the fact that there is not an ADM source in the right-hand column; or alternatively, or perhaps both, these are facts which were the subject of the litigation concerning judicial notice in which the Trial Chamber refused to judicially notice these facts. Now, those facts may or may not be considered as hypotheticals. They simply might be facts which are true but are irrelevant to these proceedings or facts which have been, as Your Honours are well aware, perhaps established by a Trial Chamber but which are currently pending on appeal. And again, the Prosecution is of the view that these are not necessarily hypothetical facts, as the Prosecution understands that term to be used, and were also -- some of these facts may or may not be within the expertise of this witness. And finally, I'm not sure it appears -- and this is why I hesitated before rising to my feet. It appears that Mr. Bourgon is going to put all seven or eight pages of these facts to the witness and see how his opinion changes, if it in fact does change, based on the totality of all these facts. And again, I'm hesitant, I was hesitant to rise to my feet, Mr. President, but I'm not sure if this is the best way to get this type of evidence before Your Honours, particularly because these facts, some of them are in evidence, some of them are not in evidence, some of them may be hypothetical facts, some of them may be facts which have yet worked their way through the Appeals Chamber, and there's a variety of different types of facts in this document, and we simply need to put our concerns about this document and the approach taken by the Defence on the record for Your Honours' consideration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The Defence will respond. The Prosecution has stated that there are certain facts mentioned that have already been admitted. These aren't hypothetical facts. There's nothing hypothetical about them. They have already been established. In addition, the Prosecution stated that in the case of certain elements, judicial notice was requested and this wasn't granted for a certain number of elements following the decision that we rendered a while ago. And the Prosecution believes that by following this procedure, you are attempting to tender into evidence certain facts that were rejected. The third point raised by the Prosecution is that the facts that you are referring to - and you have qualified them as hypothetical, but in fact these are facts that you yourself are interpreting - the witness might not be in a position to recognise these facts and have an opinion about the facts. As the witness is not present, I'll provide you with an example which is very telling: You could ask the witness to confirm or not to confirm that in the territory under control the HVO was involved in systematic ethnic cleansing. You might ask the witness to assess the conduct of the HVO in such a case. All of this might give rise to problems in that the Trial Chamber doesn't see the purpose, so you should explain to us what you are trying to prove, because when you examine a witness, the purpose of the examination is to prove something. What are you attempting to prove? If you want to prove that the report that he drafted could be amended or could have been amended if he had been aware of certain facts, if that is the case, you could summarise everything very easily and say that it seems that such and such was the case, and you could ask whether the situation such as you have described it is such that his report might be amended in light of these new elements. That would enable the witness to express his position, then. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I'll try and address the concerns of the Prosecution and the concerns the Trial Chamber has evoked. I would like to provide you with the following explanations: As far as the procedure is concerned, it's quite common and it is a procedure that is followed almost everywhere in courts when an expert witness is called to testify. The role of an expert witness is to assist the Trial Chamber, as the witness has certain expertise and can aid the Trial Chamber in performing its duties. This is knowledge or expertise that the Trial Chamber does not have and can enable the Trial Chamber to obtain additional information. In this case, the Trial Chamber agreed to hear a witness, as suggested by the Prosecution, to hear a military expert, and the Trial Chamber has authorised this witness to express his opinion, given his qualifications, to express his opinion about certain issues. What the Defence would like to do, Mr. President, is to obtain this witness's opinion, because that is the purpose for which this witness is present. We would like to hear this witness's opinion about certain issues. As I have said, this is a procedure which is used everywhere. We mention a hypothetical case, and then the witness expresses his opinion with regard to this hypothetical case. When referring to a hypothetical case, Mr. President, the case might be partially true, partly unproved, partly in dispute, but that is not what is at stake. The issue we're dealing with is to know whether the instructions given to the witness, whether the purpose is to know whether what we tell a witness of is hypothetical. We then ask the witness to take into consideration all the facts we have presented him with, and we would then ask him a couple of questions that have a direct link to his sphere of expertise. The witness may be in a position to bear in mind all these facts and to answer these questions. In our opinion, Mr. President, the witness could go even further than just confirming that his report could be amended. He could provide us with expert knowledge and expert opinion that could be new and different and he could express this opinion. As to the value of this opinion, it would have no value unless these facts were proved in whatever manner at some subsequent time. In such a case, the burden the Defence would have, if I wanted to validate this and give probative value, would be to show that this -- that these facts are actually true. If the Defence only manages to prove 75 per cent of the facts mentioned, the Trial Chamber would be in a position to determine whether these -- whether the witness would have provided the Trial Chamber with his opinion, with the opinion he provided the Trial Chamber with [as interpreted]. If all the facts are proved, the Trial Chamber would reach the conclusion that the expert's opinion is in fact very significant and has high probative value and could affect other evidence. The Trial Chamber could assess to what extent the opinion expressed by the expert witness about facts that he knows aren't true, the witness knows that these are hypothetical facts but we can ask him: If these facts are true, what is your opinion in such a case? When I go through these facts, if the witness fails to understand them, he can ask for explanations; not about the historical character of the facts but about what we're trying to illustrate by referring to certain facts. The other procedure that we could follow, Mr. President, is to go through the Defence's evidence, and that would take up two weeks of hearings. This is the procedure we have decided to follow in order to save time, because we don't think there are any surprises. All these facts have been obtained from documents and from other evidence that we want to tender into evidence, and we are sure that we will be able to tender them into evidence in order to validate the opinion of the expert witness. For these reasons, Mr. President, we believe that we should be granted leave to proceed in this manner, in order to save time. And as I'm aware of the risk - because there is a risk - as I'm aware of the risk that if these facts aren't proved in the course of the proceedings, this could affect the probative value of the opinion of expressed by the witness today. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Before I give the floor to Mr. Mundis, in order to be quite clear about this situation, the Trial Chamber would like to note that you have explained your procedure, your plan, and you have told us about the Defence's position, the Defence's strategy. As far as expertise is concerned, there are several procedures we could follow: There's your procedure, which you have just explained; and there's another efficient procedure that could be followed, and that is to ask questions -- put questions to a witness about what he has said, and the Defence, within the framework of the common-law procedure, could call another expert witness, who could repeat the same things but following the Defence's manner, and then the Trial Chamber will assess the situation. This is another procedure that could be followed. You prefer to follow the procedure you have mentioned; that is your right. On the other hand, in order to allow you to continue, you said that at the end of this procedure, you will ask the witness two questions. As the witness is not present, could you tell us about the two questions that you were going to ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I should have included that in my earlier submission. The questions that I will put to the witness have a direct link to the questions that have -- that were put to him in his report. In particular, it concerns the effect -- the impact of being in such a situation, what the impact on the command responsibility would be, on the possibility of taking measures, on the valuation of the measures that were taken. And it would concern the question as to whether it would be reasonable to proceed in such a manner in such circumstances. Other hypothetical cases could be presented today and tomorrow we could address certain other issues, but these questions are questions that have been raised in the expert's report, and they are questions that have been raised by the Prosecution. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, you understand that you have called a military expert as a witness and the Defence can counterattack with regard to the contents of the expertise if they think that the expertise -- the expert report is prejudicial to the Defence, and it's the Defence's strategy they want to proceed in this manner. What does the Prosecution have to say in the light of what Mr. Bourgon has just said?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, certainly the Prosecution does not contest in any way the right of the Defence to cross-examine the witness, nor does the Prosecution contest the right of the Defence to put hypothetical questions to the witness. Our position is that these are not necessarily hypothetical facts. We're more concerned with the procedure. Let me, in light of the comments, the final comments made by my learned friend Mr. Bourgon, let me identify the issue as the Prosecution sees it, because I think it might be a little more clear, in light of what Mr. Bourgon has said. Mr. President, assuming we follow the procedure that the Defence has started - that is, Mr. Bourgon reads the entire eight-page document to the witness and then puts a couple of questions to him concerning how his report may or may not be different in light of these facts - we are then left, Mr. President, with the dilemma of knowing which of these facts would have led the expert to change his report. Then when we get into the Defence phase and the Defence attempts to prove these facts or does perhaps prove all of these facts, or let's assume they only prove 50 per cent of them, we won't know if those are -- if those are the facts that led this expert to change his report. The only way we will know which facts led him to change his report, if in fact that is the case, is for the Defence to put each of these facts individually to the witness, in the terms of, "General Reinhardt, if you knew that Bosnia and Herzegovina was recognised as an independent state on 6 April 1992 by the EU and the United States, would your opinion have changed; yes or no?" And if, of course, he says yes, it would have changed, how would it have changed? Then to proceed to the second fact and the third fact and the fourth fact. And I understand, Mr. President, that that's a time-consuming process, but to put all of these facts to the witness, without knowing which of these facts would lead him to change his mind, means that when we get to the Defence phase and they establish, say, only half of these facts, we won't know if those are the facts that would have led this expert to change his opinion or not. It's a question of getting this procedure on the record in such a way that we all understand at the conclusion of the trial how the expert's opinion would have changed based on these facts. And if his opinion would have changed, how it would have changed, et cetera. And so that's our real concern. And I -- I understand this is a timely process, but the Prosecution would submit it's the only way that we'll be able to know which of these facts would have changed the expert's opinion, if in fact any of them would change his opinion. Of course, the other possible way of doing this, Mr. President, would be to provide these facts to the witness perhaps at the end of today's proceedings and have him come in tomorrow and explain, using a tick-box system or something, that this fact would have changed his opinion and this fact would have changed his opinion but the rest wouldn't. I'm just giving an example. That might be another way. But our position, Mr. President, particularly in light of what the Defence have said, is that we need to know which of these facts would result in a change in his opinion, and how.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Mundis. The Prosecution has clarified the debate. According to what Mr. Mundis has said, the fact that one reads out eight pages of facts to the witness might give rise to confusion, because with regard to the totality of the facts we won't know which ones are the ones that might make the witness amend his report. As a result, it might be better to refer to each fact individually and then the witness might say, "Yes, I agree," or "I don't agree," "I'll change something," et cetera. The first fact, recognising the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina, we could ask the witness whether he is aware of this or not. And then we could take note of his answer and proceed. That is one manner of proceeding. In such a case, we'll be in a position to assess the so-called hypothetical facts. The other solution suggested by the Prosecution, which would also enable us to save time, would be to show the witness the document -- to provide the witness with the document and the witness could examine it in the evening and return having ticked the relevant facts. But in such a case we won't have an adversarial debate. There are about 40 facts referred to, but we could proceed very rapidly because, given the witness's past, the witness can understand matters very quickly and answer very quickly. So you could ask the witness these questions very quickly. We could go through all the 40 questions very rapidly. What do you think about this, Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The issue raised by my colleague, Mr. President, it is that the expert provides an opinion about a given subject. The question was put to the witness, and the Defence doesn't want to go through each individual fact because when you take these facts on an individual basis, it might not affect the witness's opinion. The Defence would like to proceed by examining themes or subjects. The first subject concerns the situation; the second subject is the issue of the Mujahedin; the third subject is the issue of Dusina; the fourth one is the issue of Maljine; and finally, we have the events in Miletici. This is the procedure we wanted to follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. I'm not following you at all any more, because in the document that I have we have the heading, "The situation." There are three pages that concern the situation. That is followed by a page entitled, "Mission." Then, "The situation in Central Bosnia." It's composed of two pages; and then, "The problems encountered by the 3rd Corps." You mentioned Dusina, Maljine. Where can this be found?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, that is the first theme. We have a similar document for each subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So there's another document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely, Mr. President. This is the procedure we wanted to follow in order to save time. Because as we have already said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please show us the other documents so we can see things more clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, Mr. President, I don't have these documents with me. They are prepared, but I don't have them with me, because today I wanted to deal with the subject of the situation. And as I said at the beginning of the cross-examination, I will then go on to the question of the measures taken and then I will be referring to specific documents and tomorrow I want to deal with four other hypothetical cases. And the situation we're in at the moment, Mr. President, is that the expert witness will examine a subject, a situation. For example, if I refer to the events in Dusina - I think there are 27 facts that concern Dusina - we can present these 27 facts to the witness which concern all the events in Dusina from the beginning to the end of the relevant period. We could tell the witness, "Don't worry about whether this is true or not. That's not what's at stake. If the facts are true, what is your opinion as a military expert with regard to the events that transpired and are referred to in this document?" The witness would then give us his opinion, and it would then be for the Trial Chamber to assess the probative value of what the witness has said. Because when the expert replies to the question he won't say, "Yes, my opinion has been modified." He should say, "Yes, my opinion has been modified because of such-and-such a fact," and he would then inform the Trial Chamber of his opinion and just for the Trial Chamber to assess the response in the light of the evidence presented in the course of the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I'm concerned, I'm not at all convinced that such a procedure might be interesting for the Defence. It will take up a lot of time. And according to what you have said, the expert would only give an assessment of hypothetical events, and then you would say, "If this hypothesis was true, would you have changed your report?" So this is a procedure you would like to follow and that would take up a certain amount of the Trial Chamber's time. It's for you to conduct the defence as you see fit, but as far as judicial procedure is concerned, we have certain questions. But it is for you to conduct the cross-examination as you see fit. We are concerned about not wasting time. Above all, we don't want to cause prejudice to either of the parties. The witness can only remain here until Friday, and Friday will be the day on which the Judges will be asking the witness questions. We will follow a quite different procedure. So you still have today and tomorrow. This is how you want to proceed. We will withdraw to debate the matter, because you have raised an issue that has to do with the time we will be using, so we have to deliberate. We'll be back in a few minutes' time. --- Break taken at 11.58 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. The Chamber has deliberated regarding the question of the procedure in view of the objections presented by the Prosecution. The Chamber notes that the aim sought by the Defence was to find out whether the expert, in view of certain facts, would confirm the gist of his report or would he modify certain points after reviewing certain facts which have been described either as fictitious or real, supported by questions put by the Defence. Within this context, the Chamber notes that one difficulty emerges straight away, and that is if the expert modifies his assessment, the assessment contained in his expert report, on the basis of which facts or evidence would his assessment be modified. Therefore, the Chamber is of the opinion that in the interest of the -- of obtaining full benefit from the expert witness, that we should proceed as follows: The expert should be shown the document which you have prepared as well as the other documents and the other questions. The expert will have the rest of the afternoon and the evening to review those documents. And when the hearing is resumed tomorrow, after having time to study the documents, the expert will reply to the questions you have prepared for him and then the expert will confirm whether he stands by his report or whether certain parts of his report would be modified or amended in view of the elements contained in these documents. These documents should also be provided to the Chamber in their totality because we have to be -- have to familiarise ourselves with them; and the same applies to the Prosecution, which means that we still have time which may be used by the Defence for other questions, and tomorrow we can take the day to apply this technique, which is a little unusual, after all, so that the Defence may, in accordance with his strategy -- their strategy and their aims, put the questions to the witness. I give you the floor, Mr. Bourgon. This means that you should have in your possession all the documents -- relevant documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Defence thanks the Chamber for their ruling. We will act accordingly, and I will move on to another section which is not related to these documents, and later on we will provide the witness with these documents at the end of the day so that he can study them. Therefore, I will go on to another line of questioning now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Mundis, I hope there's no obstacle remaining, in view of the fact that you yourself suggested this procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, none whatsoever. I simply wanted to draw to the Trial Chamber's attention with respect to timing issues. As Your Honour has noted, the witness needs to depart on Friday. I do recall from meeting the witness two and a half weeks ago that he has an engagement Friday evening in Berlin, and we may need to raise the possibility of extended hours if -- if that has to happen, Mr. President, that would need to be done tomorrow afternoon, rather than extending our sitting on Friday, and I'm simply drawing that to everyone's attention, so that if we do have time pressures steps might be taken this afternoon to address with the witness and the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Regarding time, let us not forget that Mr. Kubura's Defence also needs two hours. Therefore, Mr. Bourgon, how much time will you need tomorrow roughly to apply this procedure? Because let us not forget that we need another two hours for the Defence team for Mr. Kubura, in view of the fact that Friday has been reserved for the questions of Judges, additional questions by both parties. Therefore, we must also not forget that the witness has certain engagements for Friday evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we have already taken a little time, but it was quite inevitable. But we believe that if the documents are given to the witness, we will have four series of facts. We will need about 30 minutes per series, which will mean a maximum of two hours, and then two hours will be left for my colleagues representing Mr. Kubura's Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore, in theory we will be able to complete everything tomorrow. Without any further ado, Mr. Usher, will you go and bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All the documents and the questions, please, need to be distributed at the end of today's hearing; and for us as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the questions are not in writing; however, the documents will be ready. What we could do, we have two documents with us which we can give to the witness straight away and give him all the others by the end of the day, as well as the documents -- as well as the questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, we asked you to leave. This was only because we had to discuss certain procedural problems so that we could plan our work for today, tomorrow, and Friday, in view of your own obligations. So we have agreed on a certain procedure: Documents will be given to you, which you will be able to look through at peace this afternoon and the evening; and then the Defence tomorrow will put questions to you on the basis of those documents. In this way, we will be able to save time. We are now resuming the hearing, and the Defence will have Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. another line of questions for you now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [In English] General, we will move on to a different aspect, or the next line of questioning in relation to the cross-examination based on your expert report. The next issue I wanted to raise with you was the issue of measures taken by General Hadzihasanovic. And to begin this section, I would like to refer you to paragraph 9.4.12 of your report, which is on page 27. Sorry, General, this is more 9.4.14. Do you have this report with you now?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: In this paragraph 9.4.14, you refer to the report which was sent by General Hadzihasanovic dealing with the legality in the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and that this report deals with a large number of cases forwarded to the military disciplinary court of the 3rd Command. And then you go on to say: "But there was not a single member of the 3rd Corps Command that has committed a disciplinary offence." And you quoted this from the report of 10 August 1993.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If I go -- and you go on in the same paragraph that then General Hadzihasanovic explained the situation of the two district military courts and that he commented on their legal proceedings and he basically said, "It is alarming and intolerable." Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. This is just a quotation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And he complained that there were hundreds of unfinished very difficult cases which had been there for a long time - I'm not real reading from your report but paraphrasing - including murder, rapes, and similar offences, and that can produce a catastrophic result for the enforcement of order and legality in that area and even in the combat morale. And then you go on to say: "But summarising the situation, he came to the conclusion that regarding the criminal offences that have been committed, not a single one was committed by any of the members of the 3rd Corps Command." My first question in relation to this paragraph, General, relates to footnote 151. Footnote 151 refers to the document PT1156. I would like you to read the footnote at 151 and to confirm that you were referring to the report of the Canton Court in Zenica dated 10 May 1993.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, I would say, would you agree with me that there may be a mistake because the Canton Court in Zenica did not exist in 1993?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: 2002. So this footnote, then, is not something that dates back to 1993 but that dates back to 2002.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. Concerning cases of 1992 and 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we go back to what you were saying, in terms of this document, you understand that the Canton Court did not exist in 1993, but what happened is that the Canton Court basically took over the files of the district military court.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Did you understand that from document PT1156?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And it would appear from this letter, I guess you would agree, that there was a request sent to the court, to the Zenica cantonal court, on 10 May -- the request was sent on 28 March 2002.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Are you aware of who sent this request for information to the Zenica cantonal court?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if I would refer to you to what the questions which were requested in this document, my first question was -- I guess if we go to the third paragraph -- or the second paragraph, it appears that the answer provided would cover the questions that what was the decree law on district military court, a document that you have seen, and that this is the basic document that created the Zenica district military court for the Zenica district and that this court covered the following municipalities: Kakanj, Zavidovici, Zenica, and Zepce.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that was between January of 1993 and March 1994.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So I guess one could assume, because we do not have the question, that the question raised at that time was: Was there an existing district military court in Zenica? And if so, on the basis of what document in that time frame? I can't be precise with the question, but one could assume that this was the question that was asked.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so too, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And during that period, then it says that in addition to the municipalities listed and because of the blockade of the city of Sarajevo, the court also covered additional municipalities; namely, Visoko, Breza, Vares, Olovo, and the part of Busovaca that was under BH army control.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So basically the question must have been what were the villages or the territorial jurisdiction of the Zenica district military court.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And then you've got the name of the judges, so I guess the question was: Who were the judges during this time frame?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought so too, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And we have a number of judges. And the next paragraph goes on to say that: "This court, in accordance with the instructions of the Federal Ministry of Justice, took over the documentation of the Zenica district military court."

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And the question must have been: Where are the documents from the district military court?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And then the next paragraph goes on to say that: "According to information from the register of this court, which was taken over," then they go on to cite three cases.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: First there was the case of Mirko Vlajic, and this appears to be a member of the HVO who was accused of war crimes on 9 June 1993 in accordance with Article 142 of the Criminal Code.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that this indictment was rejected.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Then it goes on to state two more cases, and I refer to the second page of the document, the case of Dzemal Zahidovic. Now, even though it is not mentioned, are you able to confirm that Dzemal Zahidovic is of Muslim origin?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what origin he is from.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Would that be an important fact for you to know in order to determine if any measures had been taken by General Hadzihasanovic against members of the Bosnian army?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, we don't know from this paragraph whether he is a member of the Bosnian army or if he maybe is a civilian, but we know that he was accused of committing a war crime against Article 142; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And the third case mentioned is that of Mr. Vinko Vidovic, and it says that he was found guilty because he committed something on 16 April 1993 and that this was, again, a war crime against the civilian population. That is correct?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. And he was a member of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Of the HVO. So on the basis of the three cases that are there, these are three war crimes cases; you would agree?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And two are members of the HVO; the first and the third. And the second, we don't know who he is.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But it would have been important for you to know if he was indeed a Muslim in order to find out the measures taken by General Hadzihasanovic.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: The letter goes on to say that: "These are three cases, and these are the only ones tried for war crimes during the period of that court's existence."

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So only three war crimes cases. And they said according with BH army members, in that period there were no BH army members who were accused of having committed a war crime.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: We can deduct this from this statement.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So for you having this information, this might have been one of the reasons that led you to conclude that actions or measures were not taken all the way by General Hadzihasanovic.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I took this here, just to support what he said before, that based on his knowledge no members of his army have committed war crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I took this as an independent source, which basically supports what he has claimed in that document before.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, that is the -- and then the letter goes on to say that whoever sent this request -- we have a fair idea, but we can't confirm who sent the request. And that's the information that was provided to yourself in assessing the question that was posed to you.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And I referred to -- back to the paragraph 9.4.14, where you talk about the 10th of August report and say he did complain about the legal system --

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: -- but he confirmed -- and you say, on two occasions, which is footnotes 150 and 151, that not a single member of the 3rd Corps Command has committed a disciplinary offence. That is footnote 150.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that at the end of the paragraph, regarding criminal offences that have been committed, not a single one was committed by any of the members of the 3rd Corps Command. Now, you understood from this paragraph, of course, that what General Hadzihasanovic was referring to was members of his headquarters. That means none of the persons in his headquarters had committed a disciplinary offence or -- or a crime.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would extend this, because for me the 3rd Corps Command encompasses all the forces under his command.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: That was your understanding --

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is my understanding of the term "3rd Corps Command."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if I was to suggest to you that "3rd Corps Command" really meant his headquarters, would that change your opinion on things?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this would somehow limit the scope of -- of what is said here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Just before the break, I would like to take this document, the August report, that was sent by General Hadzihasanovic on the legality --

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: -- and just to confirm with you what your understanding of "3rd Corps Command" was. Could you take this document, which is PT780.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I refer to you to the second paragraph, which says that: "The 3rd Corps Command analysed again the state of legality."

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: From your understanding of this sentence, is the general referring to the complete corps or to his headquarters?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: He talks about the 3rd Corps Command and subordinate command in units. In my understanding, the way this has been written, it's the entire command.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: This specific sentence, General.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not talking about -- I'm not -- I don't want to take out this specific sentence out of the context of the document. For me the context of the document basically talks about his entire command.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If we go into this document in more specific details, we see that within this document he is speaking about number and type -- I refer to, sorry, to page 2 of 8, the number and type of disciplinary offences, possibly committed criminal offences and other misdemeanours. And then he goes on to state that: "Since the military disciplinary first instance court was created this year, there were five --" and then something is missing, "...were started."

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And then he goes on to talk about the types of offences, misuse of official position, taking of military property, careless performing of military service. And then, in terms of this type of offences, then he talks about the work of the disciplinary court, and he says: "More attention should be given to the disciplinary court because it's not working quickly enough." And if we refer to the gist of his report, where you quoted himself as saying that: "There are hundreds of cases." And I quote again from your report: "There are hundreds of unfinished very difficult cases which lie there for a year." And he was talking about murder, rapes, and similar. Now, how could General Hadzihasanovic put in a letter that there is no offences committed by members of the 3rd Corps Command if your interpretation of "3rd Corps Command" is right and at the same time saying that there are hundreds of unfinished cases, including murder and rape that lie there?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe I don't understand the question, but I think a corps command, which is a rather restricted group of soldiers and NCOs and officers, normally doesn't commit war crimes. They are sitting most of the time behind their desk and doing staff jobs. And the numbers which we are just quoting here -- which you just quoted here could not have been affected by members of the staff but only of the entire area of responsibility of General Hadzihasanovic. And that again brings me back to the way that I see that he is talking about his entire corps; i.e., corps headquarters, plus the subordinate units, and not only about the corps command, i.e., the corps headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And would it be possible, General, that you are wrong in this respect and that he was referring only to his headquarters?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would never say that what I said is the Bible. I don't know whether I am absolutely right. I just tell you about my interpretation as I see this from my -- my way of reading it and interrelating it to other information I got.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And this is really a definite piece of information which led you to conclude that no measures had been taken by General Hadzihasanovic, at least up to the end, as you were saying.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I have never said that he didn't have taken any measures. You don't quote me correctly in this regard. I even refer to cases where he had taken all the measures which I think have to be taken. So I just said he was interested in what's going on in the court; he was interested also to speed it up. He was very unhappy with the situation as it has developed with the court. And there were cases which were important for him to follow up on his disciplinary -- for disciplinary reasons of his forces. And this is what I say here, and not what you just implied I had said.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But would I be right in saying that this is the information that you had with respect to at least this type of measures and that you were under the belief from this document because you had no additional information that those were the measures taken by the 3rd Corps before the Zenica district military court?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is right, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And in doing so, then this probably led you - and correct me if I'm wrong - to basically go on to the paragraph where you quoted, where it's -- I quoted this at the beginning of my cross-examination, when you were saying that he did feel responsible, he did take preventative action, but he wasn't willing to take the extra step and to punish, to ensure that crimes would not be committed again.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you take this, again, out of the context, because the context for -- for me in the whole statement is not that members, soldiers of his organic 3 Corps Command committed war crimes. We are talking specifically about the Mujahedin. And I said that he as a general said, "No soldiers of my command, which were under my direct command, committed anything like this, as far as criminal activities against human law and international law were concerned." This is the interpretation as I see this.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if, General, I think -- because I think we need to stop for the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, what time do we have to have the break? One last question, Mr. President, with your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: General, I'll show you information which is different to this which you had to show that in fact more than 1.000 reports had been filed before the Zenica district military court over the course of one year.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Would that change your views with respect to the measures taken by General Hadzihasanovic to punish and ensure that crimes would not be committed again?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can put my statement until now only on the documents and material given to me and analysed by me. If there is additional documents -- if there are additional documents, additional information pertaining to that, I'm sure willing to consider this and maybe also change my -- my position.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So, General, what I propose we do is that -- the question is: I will propose to you the same question after the break without giving you the answer as to whether there is or is there no information, asking for your opinion whether the fact that more than 1.000 cases being filed before the Zenica district military court would change your opinion on the measures taken by General Hadzihasanovic to punish people to ensure that crimes would not be committed again.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Just to get your opinion at the beginning of -- when we come back again.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we could have the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We will resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may continue, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [In English] General, we left just before the technical break on a question that I mentioned I would be putting to you at the beginning of this last session for today. Before I put the question to you, however, I -- I need to once again apologise to the translators and -- I'm sorry, to the interpreters, who have warned me yet again that I speak too quickly and that to ensure that there was a pause between myself and yourself. I apologised yesterday. I apologise again today. I will endeavour to give the interpreters sufficient time to properly do their job. So with respect to the question I wanted to put to you, General, this question was - and I will try to summarise the question - you have been given information with respect to complaints filed before the Zenica district military court --

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: -- is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And this letter state that is throughout a certain period of time there were three cases for war crimes brought before this court.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Two of which were against HVO members and one against probably a civilian that we don't know of, because we don't know whether he's a Muslim or HVO, but we know for a fact based on this letter that he was not a member of the army.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that this helped you to conclude that at least before this body there were a limited number of cases that had been brought by the 3rd Corps. And my question to you before the break was: If I would show you that in fact more than 1.000 cases were brought before this court whether this would change your mind in terms of the measures taken by General Hadzihasanovic to go the extra step and punish to ensure that all violations, any type of violation, would not be repeated again.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it would, presuming that those 1.000 cases were brought before the court by the 3rd Corps, because we know that within the 3rd Corps we had some 18 brigades, if I remember correctly, and some 16 Municipal Staff, and they also could bring forward cases like this. So I assume that the majority of those cases you're talking about, then, were brought forward by the corps headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, General, would I be right in saying that if the corps commander issues an order to his brigades and to all of his units to ensure that all criminal cases are brought forward to one of the three levels, including the disciplinary -- sorry, including the district military court, that any case brought forward by a brigade could be attributed as meaning putting into action the order of the corps commander?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with that, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, I mentioned the figure 1.000. You will agree with me that this would be probably a very high figure for a corps in a period of about 12 months to have 1.000 criminal cases. Would that be a very high number?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's a high number. In it's -- it's also reflected in many reports, when the commanders were concerned about the problems within their forces that -- and most of the -- they were disciplinary problems which have been probably handled at the corps, at that level, and they were very unhappy with the way their soldiers reacted sometimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if I would cut this figure in two, 500 would still be a very high number.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be a very high number.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, it's not the figure that is important but actually that measures were taken when a violation was brought to the attention of the commander.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you are aware of the fact, General, based on the documents that you have been given, that in addition to the Zenica district military court, there was also the Travnik military court.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: At this point in time, General, I would like to give you a series of documents that I would like to produce before this Chamber and to enter in a procedure we call for identification so that we can use these documents and ask you some questions on these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, could the usher distribute these documents. We have two binders containing a series of documents and divided on the basis of 11 different subjects. We have two series of binders, so that it's more -- it's easier for everyone to use. We have one series for you, Mr. President, and one for the binder [as interpreted]. And for the others present in the courtroom, we have prepared the same sort of document but in envelopes and divided on the basis of subjects. We'd like to apologise to the Judges because unfortunately, when we were preparing the binders, we didn't have enough binders for you. We have documents for everyone, but we only have two copies of these series of documents which are in binders. Mr. President, it is the Defence's intention to have these documents marked for identification in bundles on the basis of each subject. We will proceed on the basis of each individual theme and mark one bundle with a number for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [In English] [Previous translation continues] ... may I ask you to take this binder and to turn -- take the first binder and turn to tab number 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The interpreters suggest that to the extent that this is possible, we put the documents on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [In English] May I ask you, General, to take the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Just for clarification, when Mr. Bourgon says, "Tab 2," I assume that this would be folder 2 for those of us who don't have binders? Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: This would be folder number 2, but the theme is "Judgement by the district military court in Zenica," including 23 documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: General, if I may ask you to turn to the first document in this tab. It is a document dated 11 March of 1993 going from the 3rd Corps Command and is addressed to all subordinated command of the 3rd Corps. May I ask you, please, to take a look at this document.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Can you for the benefit of the Trial Chamber explain what is your understanding of this document.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the corps commander asks his subordinate commands that all criminal activities as far as they have been committed and have been tracked should be forwarded to his headquarters so that his headquarters is capable of seeing what happened and how the things have been followed up.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Are you able to confirm, General, based on the date of this document that this is not contemporaneous to either the events in Dusina, Miletici, or Maljine?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Can I ask you to move to the next document under this tab. This is a document dated 3 September 1993. It comes from the 3rd Corps Military Police Battalion and is addressed to the 3rd Corps chief of security. Do you have this document?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: May I ask you, General, to take a look at this document and to comment on basically what this document is about, and I would ask you to focus on paragraph 3, "Application of military police measures against members of the BH army." And also, General, on --

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not so fast, sir. I'm not so fast.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, General.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really see this for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, General.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: So, please, at least I have to have the chance to read it before I comment on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Please accept my apologies. This is a...

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And also to paragraph 4 of the same document.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, General, please to simply read the headings of the following paragraphs, beginning with paragraph 5, "Confiscated items"; and on page 4, "Escort of convoy columns and checking and escort of UNPROFOR vehicles"; on to paragraph 7, "On-site investigations and searches." Can you please, General, comment on the contents of this document.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say this is a condensed report of the Military Police Battalion of the 3rd Corps about their activities in a certain period of time and what they have done in order to endorse the discipline and morale of the BH army soldiers. They say how many people they have been -- they had taken care of, how many of those people have been forwarded as a case to the prosecutor's office, and how many things and what they have done as far as confiscation of the items is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, General, can you confirm that this report covers the activities of the Military Police Battalion for one single month?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And can you confirm that the number of criminal and disciplinary reports submitted at paragraph 4 by the Military Police Battalion?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a -- a great number; it's 32 individuals which -- whose cases have been forwarded.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sorry, I thought you were still reading. So, General, on the basis of this document, what would you conclude about measures being taken to punish members of the 3rd Corps for violations, whether they be disciplinary or criminal?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I see this document for the first time, and it shows that the military police, at least -- and I don't go for all these checkpoints and these things -- and the escorts, but the disciplinary cases and the consequences taken out of them and the criminal offences, like plundering and robbing, took their case very seriously.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And I would ask you, General, to turn to the third document under this tab. This is a report forwarded by the Military Police Battalion of the 3rd Corps, which is addressed to the security sector of the 3rd Corps and dated 20 March 1994, and the subject is, "The report on criminal reports filed." Do you have this document, General?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Can you please look at the contents of this report.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only can scan it, I think, during that period of time, but there are quite a few cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Can you confirm that at paragraph (c) on page 1 we are talking about 295 soldiers of the BH army were the subject of a criminal report and 17 officers of the BH army, and that covers the period from 14 September 1992 to 1 March 1994?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And looking at paragraph (d), the structure of crimes, I would ask you to follow me from crime to crime for at least the first couple, and whether you can confirm that we have a case for aggravated theft, theft of a weapon or piece of combat equipment; that we have eight reports filed for involuntary manslaughter; and that on the next page - I will simply refer to the first three categories - "incorrect and careless handling of an assigned weapon"; "assault of a military personnel in the course of their duties"; "false impersonation"; and finally "murder" for 16 reports. Would it be fair to say, General, that the report of the Military Police Battalion for this period shows that they did take their duties very seriously and that they applied the orders issued by the commanding general, Enver Hadzihasanovic, commander of the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: May I ask you, General, to turn to tab 11, which is in the second binder that has been provided to you. Under this tab, General, you only have a list of documents, and I would ask the court usher to bring document DH119, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, the Defence has requested document DH119.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If I may be of assistance to the registry, I believe that I provided you with a list of five documents that I would like to show the witness one by one.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: General, can you please take a look at this document dated 10 January 1994, which is a report on the work of the Travnik district military prosecutor's office for 1993.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Can you, General - and I understand this is a four-page document - I would like to draw your attention to the second paragraph, where it says that: "The prosecutor's office is a newly formed organ." Do you have the same document that I have?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm just with the second paragraph starting: "When carrying out his basic functionary."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sorry, I was talking about the third paragraph. It was the second after number 1. Sorry, General.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: "However --"

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Starting with "however."

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: "However, it should be stressed that this prosecutor's office is a newly formed organ which began in 1993 and that this paragraph highlights difficulties encountered by the prosecutor's office."

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that the next paragraph stresses also other difficulties and that of other judicial organs and law enforcement organs which did not keep the pace for the work of the district military prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. This is somehow almost in the same direction as the complaint of General Hadzihasanovic in August of the year before.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that when we go on to the page 2, I would like to mention -- to draw your attention to the fourth paragraph, where it says: "Turning to cooperation of the security organs of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina Armed Forces, military police, there are big differences in this. In fact, cooperation is outstanding on occasions. However, there are also cases of turning a blind eye as well as attempts of commanders to overrule the organs of military justice. Although this has been completely prevented in work to date."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could a copy be placed under the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the fact that in some cases commanders are not satisfied with the rapidity with which the Office of the Prosecutor is working or that those commanders were in pitch battle operations that prevented them from cooperating better.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this -- just a minute. Yeah. I can't read it any more. If I read this directly, it talks about the beginning of the operations when it was very difficult, and it has changed in the meantime. And it's difficult because as he says, the commander sometimes had a blind eye towards all these cases. But we also have cases, at least in the documents which I saw, that the military police didn't do their job properly. They started plundering and looting themselves and tried to get as much out of the pie as upon. So sometimes they were just not doing their job appropriately, and that's what he says here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And in this document, this paragraph -- the next paragraph down says that: "The criminal reports submitted to this prosecutor's office are generally incomplete and have certain deficiencies."

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just have a look, because it's not here in --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Oh, sorry.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: A little bit technically complicated, but we'll find a way. Okay, I've got this.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And would that be -- would it be a fair statement to say that this could be a direct result of the fact that the people working within the army on the legal side lacked the proper qualifications to do their work properly?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could be that they lacked the proper qualifications. It also could be that they were just not enough in manning the spaces they were supposed to man.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if I turn to the next page of this document, General, on page 3.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which paragraph, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Page 3, just under the heading, "2. Criminal reports received." And I read with you: "In the report period, the prosecutor's office received a total of 823 criminal reports concerning 1.044 persons and measures prescribed by law were undertaken for all reports received, in other words, proceedings were initiated."

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Would it be a fair statement to say that this office did all of the work that it was supposed to do when being seized of a report coming from the military?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, it looks like.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And as we confirmed this morning, when the commander did file a report or send the report to the district military prosecutor, for all intents and purposes he had fulfilled his duty and he was basically ready to have whoever the perpetrators were punished with the intent of stopping this type of criminal behaviour.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm absolutely with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'd like show the witness document DH120, 120. And I'd like to show the witness the first document, because there are six documents under the heading "DH120." And I would simply ask you, General, to look at every one of these documents and confirm that you have six monthly reports and that there is a figure of criminal reports filed in each of these reports on a monthly basis.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Would it be fair to conclude, General, on the basis of these reports that, one, monthly reports were filed by that office, but that there was regular and continuous judicial activity coming from reports which were filed to the district military prosecutor's office?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. From November on onwards. These are the things.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I would like to have the witness shown document DH121, please.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is like Christmas.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: General, can you confirm that you have a document --

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Oh, sorry.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS REINHARDT [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're still struggling to get the document. Now I have a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
